headline: Issue one certificate carrying two signatures, so a PKI can change algorithms without reissuing to everyone at once.
summary: A PKI moving to post-quantum algorithms cannot reissue to every relying party on the same day. ITU-T X.509 (2019) clause 9.8 lets a certificate carry a second public key, a second signature algorithm and a second signature in extensions: a relying party that has not migrated reads the native signature and ignores the rest, and one that has reads the alternative signature instead. `pki.altSig` verifies that second signature, and `pki.x509.sign` and `pki.crl.sign` produce it.

Added: `pki.x509.sign` takes `issuer.altKey` beside the issuing key, with `issuer.altPublicKey` and `extensions.subjectAltPublicKeyInfo` naming the issuer's and the subject's alternative keys, and emits all three extensions. Clause 7.2.2 fixes an order that is easy to get wrong and expensive to get wrong: the alternative signature is generated first, over the certificate WITHOUT it and without the outer signature, and the native signature then covers the certificate WITH it. Signing in the other order leaves a native signature that does not cover the alternative one. The verb does both passes, so the order is not the caller's to arrange. `altSignatureAlgorithm` is resolved from the alternative key and `altSignatureValue` is computed, so supplying either is refused rather than emitted unchecked, and either half of the mechanism without the other is refused, which clause 7.2.2 requires.

`pki.crl.sign` takes `issuer.altKey` for the same mechanism on a CRL, which clause 7.10.3 gives the same procedure and the same two extensions. `subjectAltPublicKeyInfo` is not emitted on a CRL, the NOTE in clause 7.2.2 stating it is a certificate extension only.

`pki.altSig.signedData` builds the bytes an alternative signature covers. Clause 7.2.2 states them as the structure with the outer signature component and the `altSignatureValue` extension both removed, and requires a verifier to rebuild that encoding, since it never appears on the wire. This is the one place the toolkit re-encodes what it parsed, and it is done by keeping the original bytes of every component retained and recomputing only the three SEQUENCE headers whose lengths change: nothing is re-serialized from a decoded model, because a model that normalized any byte would either fail every verification or accept an encoding the issuer never signed.

`pki.altSig.verify` checks that signature under the issuer's alternative public key, which clause 9.8.4 requires, through the same engine certification-path validation uses. The algorithm is not derived: the structure states it in `altSignatureAlgorithm`, and that stated algorithm is bound to the key through the same machinery, so a key that does not match the stated algorithm resolves `false` rather than being read under some other algorithm. A structure that states no alternative signature throws rather than resolving `false`, since there is nothing to check and a `false` would read as a signature that failed.

`pki.altSig.subjectAltPublicKey` reads a certificate's own alternative public key, which is the key that verifies a certificate this one issued. `SubjectAltPublicKeyInfo` carries the same two components in the same order as `SubjectPublicKeyInfo`, and a field name is not encoded, so the extension value is an SPKI on the wire and is returned unchanged rather than rebuilt from its parts.

`pki.schema.x509.parse` and `pki.schema.crl.parse` decode the three extensions through the shared decoders, holding an alternative key and an alternative signature to whole octets and refusing an empty one. `pki.inspect.certificate` reports each by its algorithm and its length, which for a post-quantum key and signature is thousands of octets and is the case the extensions exist for.

`pki.lint.certificate` gains the `x509-altsig` profile. Clause 9.8.3 states the pairing of `altSignatureAlgorithm` with `altSignatureValue` as a shall, and clause 7.2.2 requires a certificate carrying the mechanism to carry all three, so both are graded as errors. Criticality is stated only in NOTEs recommending non-critical, with the clauses saying either is permitted, so a critical extension is graded as a warning and still parses: grading a NOTE as an error would report a requirement level the text does not state.
